```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png")
```

phwstyle applies the Public Health Wales (PHW) and CDSC house style to R
outputs. You write your analysis as usual, then add one function to brand it.

```{r}
library(phwstyle)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Colours

`phw_colours` holds every brand colour. `phw_pal()` returns palettes:

```{r}
phw_pal()                 # navy, teal, orange, pink: the default chart colours
phw_pal(5, "blues")       # sequential, for maps and heat tables
```

```{r, fig.height = 3}
show_phw_palettes()
```

Every function that takes a `palette` also accepts your own vector of
colours, e.g. `scale_colour_phw_d(palette = c("#285087", "#FF5D0C"))`.

## Colour-blind readers

About 1 in 12 men can't tell some reds and greens apart. The `accessible`
palette stays distinct for all three common types of colour blindness. Use
it everywhere with one line:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
use_phw_ggplot(palette = "accessible")  # or options(phwstyle.palette = "accessible")
```

Check any set of colours, and see them as a colour-blind reader would:

```{r}
phw_check_colours("accessible")
```

```{r, fig.height = 3}
show_phw_palettes(c("main", "accessible", "rag", "rag_accessible"), cvd = "deutan")
```

Colour should never be the only cue. Add `scale_shape_phw()` or
`scale_linetype_phw()` to charts. `phw_flextable_heat(palette = "rag")` adds
shapes to RAG cells, and `"rag_accessible"` uses navy for "good" instead of
green. `theme_phw(accessible = TRUE)` makes text and lines
larger.

## Colours that stay with their groups

If colours follow the order of the groups, adding a new group (say a new age
band) shifts every colour after it. A colour key fixes each group's colour
instead. New groups get the next free colour, and existing ones never move.

```{r}
ages <- c("0-4", "5-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+")
phw_colour_key(ages, "age_vignette")
phw_colour_key(c("Under 1", ages, "Unknown"), "age_vignette")
```

Use the key in a chart with `scale_colour_phw_d(key = "age_vignette")`, in
tables with `phw_flextable_groups()` or `phw_reactable(group_col = )`, and in
plotly with `colors = phw_colour_key(...)`. To keep keys across sessions and
reports, save them to a file in your project:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
phw_key_file("phw-colours.csv")
```

Keys store the colours themselves, so changing palette later only affects new
groups. `phw_key_recolour()` moves a whole key to a new palette on purpose.

```{r, include = FALSE}
phw_key_reset("age_vignette")
```

## ggplot2

Add `theme_phw()` to a plot, or call `use_phw_ggplot()` once to style every
plot in the session. The source line goes in the caption, the way PHW
reports show it.

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(title = "Engine size and fuel economy",
       x = "Engine size (litres)", y = "Miles per gallon",
       caption = phw_caption("ggplot2::mpg")) +
  theme_phw() +
  scale_colour_phw_d()
```

Use `theme_phw(grid = "x")` for horizontal bars and `theme_phw_map()` for
maps. `phw_finalise()` adds the logo and source footer to a chart that will
be shared on its own, and `phw_save()` saves it at report size.

## Extension packages and multi-plot figures

Charts from ggplot2 extensions (ggalluvial, ggsankey, ggridges, ggrepel,
treemapify, ggtext and others) take the PHW colour scales and colour keys like
any other chart. `use_phw_ggplot()` also restyles their own defaults (fonts,
text colours, grey fills and black outlines) through `phw_style_extensions()`.
Load those packages before calling it.

To put several charts in one figure, use `phw_arrange()` (built on patchwork)
for one PHW title and source line across all panels. For gridExtra or cowplot,
`phw_title_grob()` gives a matching title. `phw_finalise()` adds the logo footer
to any of these.

## Tables

```{r}
tbl <- data.frame(Area = paste("Area", LETTERS[1:3]),
                  Count = c(12L, 28L, 1L), Value = c(2.0, 5.5, 0.7))
phw_flextable(tbl, caption = "Table caption", source = "Example data",
              bold_first_col = TRUE)
```

`phw_reactable()` and `phw_plotly()` do the same for interactive tables and
charts. `phw_plotly()` works with any plotly chart type, including bars,
donuts, heatmaps (with `phw_plotly_colorscale()`), box plots and
`subplot()` figures.

### Summary and epidemiology tables

Five builders make the tables PHW reports use most. Each returns a data
frame that renders properly with both `phw_flextable()` and
`phw_reactable()`:

- `phw_summary_table()`: characteristics (age group, sex, risk factors...)
  as n (%) or median (IQR), optionally split by a group with a total column.
- `phw_crosstab()`: counts by two variables, with totals and row or column
  percentages.
- `phw_rate_table()`: rates per 100,000 with exact Poisson confidence
  intervals, for several demographic or risk variables at once.
- `phw_risk_table()`: attack rates and relative risks by exposure, as used
  in outbreak investigations.
- `phw_group_table()`: counts (or any statistic) from a raw data frame with
  nested row groups, such as group then type, and optional nested column
  groups, such as year then quarter. Each group row can show its group's
  total; you can add a table total and totals of the inner groups across
  all groups, and choose an indented or column layout.

```{r}
dat <- data.frame(
  group = sample(c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C"), 300, TRUE),
  type = sample(c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"), 300, TRUE),
  year = sample(2023:2024, 300, TRUE))
phw_flextable(phw_group_table(dat, rows = c("group", "type"), cols = "year",
                              labels = list(group = "Group", type = "Type", year = "Year")))
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)
ll <- data.frame(
  age_group = sample(c("0-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+"), 200, TRUE),
  sex = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 200, TRUE),
  outcome = sample(c("Outcome X", "Outcome Y"), 200, TRUE))
phw_flextable(phw_summary_table(ll, by = "outcome",
                                labels = list(age_group = "Age group", sex = "Sex")))
```

For extra column formats, use `phw_flextable_heat()` and
`phw_flextable_bars()` in flextable, and `phw_col_bar()`, `phw_col_heat()`,
`phw_col_rag()` and `phw_col_percent()` in reactable.

## Maps

`phw_boundaries()` downloads boundaries for any level of Welsh geography and
keeps a copy in your cache folder, so later calls work offline.
`phw_boundary_levels()` lists the levels: country, health boards, local
authorities, GP clusters, Senedd and UK Parliament constituencies, electoral
wards, communities, MSOAs, LSOAs, output areas, and fire and police areas.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hb <- phw_boundaries("health_board")
ggplot(hb) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = name), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_phw_d() +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(caption = attr(hb, "attribution"))
```

Join your data on the `code` column (ONS codes such as W11000028), or on
`name`. The list of releases is updated when ONS or the Welsh Government
publish new boundaries.

## More outputs

- Public health charts: `phw_epicurve()`, `phw_pyramid()`, `phw_funnel()`
  and `phw_spc()` return ordinary ggplots.
- gt and gtsummary: `phw_gt()` renders any data frame or summary table, and
  `use_phw_gtsummary()` styles every gtsummary table.
- Interactive: `phw_datatable()` for searchable tables, and `phw_leaflet()`
  with `phw_leaflet_polygons()` for maps.
- Exports: `phw_write_xlsx()` for Excel, and `phw_pptx()` with
  `phw_add_slide()` for PowerPoint.

The documentation website has a guide for each, and a gallery naming the
functions behind every example.

## Documents

- R Markdown: `output: phwstyle::phw_html_document`, `phw_word_document`
  or `phw_pdf_document`.
- Quarto: run `use_phw_quarto()` in your project, then use `format: phw-html`,
  `phw-docx`, `phw-typst`, `phw-pdf`, `phw-revealjs` or `phw-dashboard`.
- Shiny: `phw_page_navbar()` or `theme = phw_bs_theme()`.

## Wording

Every label phwstyle writes can be changed. For example:

```{r}
phw_caption("Example data", date = as.Date("2026-11-03"))
phw_caption("Example data", source_prefix = "Data: ", note = "Provisional figures")
```

## Changing anything else

Each function passes extra arguments to the function it wraps, so you can
override any default: `theme_phw(plot.title = element_text(size = 18))`,
`phw_reactable(data, pagination = FALSE)`, `phw_plotly(p, hovermode = "x")`,
`phw_bs_theme(primary = "#24A2B5")`.

## Logos

The PHW logo is a trade mark. `phw_logo()` finds it in your
`phwstyle.logo_dir` option, bundled with the package, or in a copy saved by
`phw_download_logos()`. Without a logo, outputs are still branded, just
without the logo.
